findings.title: Issuer (iss) claim accepts an array of strings, allowing issuer-validation bypass by spoofing
findings.evidence: The `allowedIss` option builds a claim validator at line 475 (`validators.push({ type: 'string', claim: 'iss', allowed: ensureStringClaimMatcher(allowedIss) })`) that, unlike `aud` at line 471, is not marked `array: true`, yet nothing in the validation path rejects an array-valued `iss`. Data flow from the attacker-controlled token: decoder.js lines 31-44 JSON-parse the payload; verifyToken reads `payload[claim]` at line 210, and lines 211-212 do `const arrayValue = Array.isArray(value); const values = arrayValue ? value : [value]`, so an array `iss` is spread into `values` and passed with `arrayValue=true` to `validateClaimValues` at line 226. That function's check at line 159 is `if (!values.some(v => allowed.some(a => a.test(v))))`, i.e. ANY one matching element makes the whole claim pass, and `validateClaimType` (lines 144-152, called at line 221 with the validator's `array` flag rather than the actual `arrayValue`) only verifies every element is a string. Consequently a signed JWT whose payload contains `iss: ['https://attacker.example/', 'https://valid-iss']` is accepted when the verifier was configured with `allowedIss: 'https://valid-iss'`, and the resulting verified `payload.iss` is the attacker-controlled array. This is CVE-2025-30144 / GHSA-gm45-q3v2-6cf8 (fixed in fast-jwt 5.0.6 by requiring non-array claims such as jti/iss/sub/nonce to match on every value, or by rejecting arrays unless `array: true`); the same loose-match path also affects jti, sub and nonce. Precondition: the attacker can present a token whose signature is valid for a key the verifier accepts (for example the documented get-jwks flow where the token's `iss`/`kid` drives key discovery); the bypass then defeats the intended single-issuer pinning and lets the attacker embed their own issuer in the accepted claim.
